new_statements.translation: b) Accent. 1. Two-syllable words: the accent generally falls on the 'second' syllable when the word has a prefix (e.g. a-, e-, i-, etc.), e.g. EROT 'path', ATOM 'gun', IŊOK 'dog'. When there is no prefix the accent generally falls on the 'first' syllable, e.g. ORI 'when', AI 'where', etc. 2. Three-syllable words: unfortunately there is no fixed rule. Some carry the accent on the last syllable (e.g. EKILÉ 'man'); others on the second syllable (e.g. ABERU 'woman'). 3. Words of more than three syllables: they generally carry the accent on the last syllable (e.g. EMOTOTÓ 'banana'; EKETATAMAN 'teacher').
new_statements.citation: Roncari, G. & M. Mantovani. [1973]. Appunti di grammatica Karimojong. Gulu (Uganda): Catholic Press [Editrice cattolica]. 263 pp.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: I re-rendered (5-page Rosetta Project scan; scan page 4 = book p. 8, headed 'b) Accento') and compared the page image word by word with the reported quote: it is verbatim (IŊOK, 'non c'e regola fissa', EKILE', ABERU, EMOTOTO', EKETATAMAN all as printed; the only differences are dropped italics on the 'Parole con.. sillabe:' headings). The supporting remarks are also as reported: p. 7 'Dittonghi e vocali doppie' (final unaccented i/e of a diphthong fades; only AI/OI may carry a final accented I, AKAI' = casa, MOI' = domani; doubled vowels aa/oo/uu/ii/ee written double 'poiche l'accento cade su entrambe'), and p. 8 'Vocale eufonica' ('La vocale eufonica unitiva e solitamente l'ultima d…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No single positional rule: accent is never on the gender/infinitive prefix; in prefixed disyllables and in words of four or more syllables it usually falls on the final syllable, prefixless disyllables are initial-accented, and trisyllables are lexically split between final and second-syllable accent ('no fixed rule'). Net picture: lexically variable accent with a strong word-final tendency (the euphonic-vowel note on p. 8 also presupposes that the accented vowel is usually the word's last).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. (p. 7 says written double vowels aa/oo/uu/ii/ee are so written 'because the accent falls on both doubled vowels', i.e. length/prominence conflated; no rhythmic or secondary accent described.)
new_statements.exceptions: Trisyllables explicitly have no fixed rule (EKILE' final vs ABERU second syllable); prefixless disyllables (ORI, AI) are initial rather than final; only the diphthongs AI and OI may bear a final accented I (AKAI' 'house', MOI' 'tomorrow'), other word-final diphthongs accent their first vowel (p. 7).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, isolated citation forms (nouns cited with their gender prefix, infinitives with aki-). Impressionistic missionary description in Italian school-grammar terms ('accento'); tone is not mentioned anywhere in the phonology chapter, although the modern literature (Novelli 1985 via Lesley-Neuman 2007:13; Vossen 1982:180-181) describes Karimojong as a three-tone (H/M/L) language, so the 'accento' heard by the authors may be pitch prominence. The Turkana catalog record (turk1308) parks an almost identical hedged syllable-count note from Barrett 1988 as secondary for the same reason.
new_statements.identity_note: Roncari & Mantovani 1973 describe Karimojong proper as taught by the Comboni (Verona) Fathers at Moroto/Gulu, Uganda = kara1483; examples are standard Ngakarimojong nouns with gender prefixes. Bader 2008 (list of works to obtain) explicitly uses 'karimojong' as a cover term for Karimojong plus Jie and Dodos (kara1483 dialects) and also Turkana (turk1308), Toposa (topo1242), Nyangatom (nyan1315) and Jiye, so any statement taken from it later needs a dialect check. Vossen 1982's Karimojong data are Koehler's 1970 200-word list only.

new_statements.quote: 2b. Stress. Stress falls normally on the Stem syllable of words. In BARI there is significant shifting of stress in certain circumstances: [...] On other occasions it is hard to determine whether tone or stress is the dominant factor: [...] Observation. Although tone and stress patterns play such a large role in grammar, the patterns themselves may vary widely even between dialects. [2a. Tone:] There are three main level tones—High, Mid, and Low, though Mid tone may often be regarded as lowered High; there is also a Falling tone which seems to constitute a separate toneme. [...] in the TESO Group, MAASAI and KALENJIN Case is also distinguished by Tone (§ 7)— but not in BARI.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Roncari & Mantovani 1973 statement (accent on the second syllable when the word has a prefix a-/e-/i-, on the first syllable when it has none): both amount to stress on the first stem syllable. Tucker & Bryan give the morphological generalization ('the Stem syllable') at the level of the whole Paranilotic group and add the tone inventory (three levels + falling), but they do not single out Karimojong, so the statement covers it only implicitly.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Paranilotic (Eastern Nilotic) languages as a group — Bari, Lotuho, Teso (Karimojong, Turkana, Toposa only as 'notes' under Teso), Maasai, Kalenjin — stress falls on the stem syllable, i.e. on the first syllable of the stem after the gender/number prefix (a-, e-, i-, aki-..), not on the prefix. The languages are tonal: three level tones (High, Mid, Low, Mid often a lowered High) plus a falling toneme, tone being lexical and grammatical (in the Teso group case is also marked by tone). No Karimojong-specific stress statement is made; Karimojong is named in the chapter only for a consonant correspondence (Teso s = Karimojong/Turkana/Toposa dh) and the verb prefix aki-.
new_statements.exceptions: Only for BARI (not Karimojong): stress shifts to a later stem syllable under emphasis (nan lo 'totogu I am cutting vs nan lo to'togu emphatic), and in some forms it is hard to say whether tone or stress is dominant; the Observation adds that tone/stress patterns can differ even between dialects (Nandi vs Kipsigis example). Footnote 1 contrasts PAKOT kara ku:kat 'with no slurring'.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan treat Karimojong only as 'some notes on KARIMOJONG, TURKANA, TOPOSA' attached to TESO inside Section 31 'The Paranilotic Languages' (pp. 443ff; Karimojong informant J. W. L. Akol); the stress statement is a generalization over Bari, Lotuho, Teso, Maasai and Kalenjin, with Bari examples only. The book's note 'Source: Questionnaire (translated from English into KARIMOJONG) filled in by informants.. sent in by Mrs. Dyson-Hudson' belongs to TEPETH (So) in chapter 29 'TEUSO', p. 392, and is not about Karimojong; likewise the fragments 'Tone is not marked throughout. Nothing is known about Stress' (Tama) and 'Neither tone nor stress is marked in most of the examples' (a Teuso-chapter language) concern other languages.

sources.note: p. 8 'b) Accento': disyllables with a gender/infinitive prefix are accented on the 2nd (final) syllable, prefixless disyllables on the 1st; trisyllables 'no fixed rule' (final EKILE' or 2nd ABERU); words of 4+ syllables 'generally' final (EMOTOTO'). p. 7: doubled written vowels (DAADANG, EDOO) because 'the accent falls on both'; final unaccented i/e of diphthongs fades; p. 8 euphonic linking vowel is usually the last vowel of the preceding word 'where the accent falls'. No mention of tone.
